relations.myth: Sanatkumāra teaches Nārada and is called Skanda
relations.note: The Upaniṣad explicitly identifies the teacher Sanatkumāra with Skanda.

relations.myth: Buddhist Skanda becomes an armored monastery guardian
relations.note: East Asian Buddhism developed transmitted Skanda traditions into the guardian Weituo.
The Vedic Kumāra antecedent is described as Prajāpati’s fiery offspring.
In the Svāhā cycle, Skanda is produced from Agni’s collected seed.
Agni transmits Śiva’s seed through the birth sequence leading to Skanda.
Svāhā collects Agni’s seed and deposits it, thereby producing Skanda.
Śiva’s uncontainable seed initiates Skanda’s epic and Purāṇic birth.
Pārvatī is Skanda’s intended and theological mother in developed Śaiva tradition.
Pārvatī gives her son the spear used against Sūrapadman.
Gaṅgā bears or cools Śiva’s seed before depositing it among reeds.
The six or seven star goddesses nurse Skanda as collective foster-mothers.
Early Tamil tradition describes the victory goddess Korravai as Murukaṉ’s mother.

relations.myth: Indra attacks the alarming divine child
relations.note: Indra assaults Skanda but fails to destroy him.

relations.myth: Indra installs Skanda as divine commander
relations.note: After attacking him, Indra recognizes Skanda and installs him as commander.
Indra gives his daughter or ward Devasenā to Skanda in marriage.
One epic account has Skanda rescue or receive Devasenā.
Skanda marries Devasenā, daughter or ward of Indra.
Viśākha emerges from Skanda’s wound or divided body as a second youth.

relations.myth: Skanda and Viśākha appear as distinct figures
relations.note: Epic narrative and Kushan coins can present Viśākha beside Skanda.
Later tradition absorbs the once-distinguishable Viśākha as a name of Skanda.

relations.myth: Three divine youths appear together on coinage
relations.note: Kushan coinage presents Mahāsena alongside Skanda-Kumāra and Viśākha.
Later consolidation treats Mahāsena as a name or form of Skanda.
Skanda’s birth causes the sages’ wives to be falsely accused of infidelity.
Skanda accepts the child-afflicting Mothers into his following and defines their powers.
The dangerous divine Mothers become members of Skanda’s following.
Skanda humiliates or imprisons Brahmā after finding his explanation inadequate.

relations.myth: Skanda teaches Śiva the meaning of Oṃ
relations.note: At Swamimalai, Skanda makes his father approach as a disciple.

relations.myth: Śiva offers a fruit of knowledge
relations.note: Śiva offers a fruit to whichever son can circle the world first.
Developed Śaiva family mythology makes Gaṇeśa Kartikeya’s brother.

relations.myth: The brothers compete for the fruit
relations.note: Gaṇeśa circles their parents while Kartikeya circles the physical world.
Gaṇeśa becomes a wild elephant so disguised Murukaṉ can rescue Valli.
Valli, the hunter-princess, becomes Murukaṉ’s regional Tamil consort.

relations.myth: Murukaṉ courts Valli in several disguises
relations.note: Murukaṉ repeatedly propositions Valli as hunter, ascetic, or other disguised figure.

relations.myth: Disguised Murukaṉ stages an elephant rescue
relations.note: Murukaṉ conceals his identity and uses Gaṇeśa’s elephant disguise to secure Valli’s promise.
Some Tamil genealogies make Viṣṇu Murukaṉ’s father-in-law through his consorts.
Murukaṉ’s early Tamil mother Korravai was later equated with Durgā or Pārvatī.

relations.myth: Kaumārī fights among the goddess’s Mātṛkās
relations.note: Kaumārī is the female power or śakti corresponding to Kumāra.

relations.myth: Skanda kills Tāraka with the spear
relations.note: Skanda kills the demon vulnerable only to Śiva’s son.

relations.myth: Skanda pierces Krauñca with his spear
relations.note: Skanda pierces Krauñca, variously understood as mountain, demon, or both.
Murukaṉ defeats Sūrapadman after a prolonged war against his forces.
Murukaṉ transforms the demon’s halves into his peacock mount and cock banner.
Murukaṉ defeats Siṃhamukha during the mature Tamil war cycle.
The Tamil war cycle includes Tārakāsura among Sūrapadman’s defeated brothers or allies.

relations.myth: Idumban challenges the child ascetic at Palani
relations.note: Murukaṉ fights Idumban when the latter attempts to move the two hills.
Murukaṉ kills Idumban during their struggle at Palani.
After killing Idumban, Murukaṉ restores him at divine request.
The restored Idumban serves as guardian and patron of burden-bearing devotees.
Skanda as Sanatkumāra guides Nārada toward knowledge of bhūman.

relations.myth: Nārada arranges Murukaṉ’s courtship of Valli
relations.note: Later Valli narratives make Nārada the divine matchmaker for Murukaṉ.
